newsitem.title: INDIA: India government plunges into crisis as ally quits.
newsitem.headline: India government plunges into crisis as ally quits.

text.p: India plunged into political crisis on Sunday after the Congress party withdrew its make-or-break support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
The bombshell announcement overshadowed delicate peace talks between India and Pakistan and threatened to stall Deve Gowda's budget for fiscal 1997/98, still to be approved by parliament.
Indian stock prices dropped sharply in off-market kerb deals on fears that Deve Gowda's shaky ten-month-old government might have to resign and call a snap mid-term election.
The ruling United Front coalition said it would stand firm.
"There is no question of the resignation of Mr Deve Gowda," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters.

Reddy was speaking after Congress President Sitaram Kesri told a hurriedly summoned news conference: "I met the President (Shankar Dayal Sharma) today and told him that we are withdrawing support to the United Front government and I also staked our claim to form a (new) government."
Kesri's letter to President Sharma said law and order had "completely collapsed."

"Lack of coordination, direction and will to govern have created a situation of drift. Communal, divisive and separatist forces are raising their heads in almost every part of the country and there is no serious effort to arrest this," the letter said.
Stockbrokers in the commercial centre Bombay said it was unclear how Congress, which has only 142 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha or lower house of parliament, would form a government.
"If Congress is taking a gamble on this one, it will be interesting to see how they will come out," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
Some brokers predicted a steep plunge on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Monday.
"This is something totally unexpected. There's trouble ahead that doesn't look like it will be easily resolved," said Ravi Gopalakrishnan, head of sales at UBS Securities.

Kesri, who became Congress president in September after former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao was forced to resign the post over corruption charges, was expected to formally stake his claim before Sharma on Monday, Congress politicians said.
But he did not appear to have the backing of several key Congress leaders, including influential former defence minister Sharad Pawar.
The United News of India quoted Pawar, regarded as a supporter of Deve Gowda's government, as saying he was not aware of the Congress decision to bring down the government.
The ruling alliance looked more united with nearly all its key constituents, including Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress, saying they fully backed Deve Gowda.

The decision-making Steering Committee of the United Front was due to meet on Monday to decide its strategy, including a likely plea to Sharma to allow Deve Gowda to face parliament when it resumes its budget session on April 21, Reddy said.
India's oldest political machine, Congress is reeling from a string of financial scandals dogging its leading politicians.
Congress officials said the withdrawal decision followed "attempts by the United Front" to split the Congress party in the key north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.

The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) formed a coalition government in the state earlier this month, thwarting Congress attempts to rule the crucial region which sends 85 deputies to the 545-member lower house of parliament.
Deve Gowda's alliance which groups free-traders, communists and centrists and controls some 178 deputies in the lower house was formed in June 1996 after inconclusive national elections.
